verses.1: Al-Mizan reads the opening as oaths by the winds that scatter dust, rain-clouds laden with water, ships gliding on the sea, and angels dispensing the divine command. Though God's command to create and govern is one, it branches as each angelic group carries it out according to its particular function, until it reaches angels connected with particular phenomena. The sequence thus gathers examples of governance on land, sea, and air under the angels, the intermediaries of that governance; a report from Imām ʿAlī gives the same interpretation. Al-Rāzī's proposal that all four oaths concern winds is judged far-fetched and less eloquent. The oath's object is that the Qur'an's or Prophet's promise of Resurrection and recompense, good for good and evil for evil, is ṣādiq, with truthfulness figuratively attributed to the promise, and that dīn, meaning jazāʾ, will certainly occur.

verses.7: Al-Mizan records ḥubuk as beauty, skilful creation, or trails like those left on wind-stirred water, and prefers the last because the oath suits people's divergent paths. Their qawl mukhtalif is most aptly their contradictory denials of the Qur'an and its promises of Resurrection and Recompense: they alternatively call it magic, nonsense, soothsaying, poetry, or ancient legends. It therefore takes 'turned away from it' primarily as turning from the Book containing that promise, while the reading that it refers to the Prophet has effectively the same result. Readings that make it the promised matter or religion are similar; the construction in which differing opinions themselves turn people away is viable, but the claim that the addressees include believers and unbelievers is not supported by the context.

verses.10: Al-Mizan prefers to understand kharrāṣūn not simply as liars but as people who speak conjecturally without knowledge while denying Resurrection and Recompense; 'Perish' invokes their deprivation of success. Their ghamrah is an ignorance that covers them as water covers a place, and their sahw is unawareness of the reality disclosed to them. Their question about when the Day of Retribution will be is derisive and asks for its hastening, though it treats the promised event as temporally located, as ordinary speech also asks when an event occurs in relation to other times.

verses.13: Al-Mizan identifies those tormented in the Fire as the preceding kharrāṣūn and notes that fatan, originally testing gold in fire, came to mean burning and punishment. Rather than disclose the Day's date, which belongs to the Unseen and is known only to God (7:187), the verse answers by describing their condition: the Day of Retribution is when they are punished in the Fire.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains this as God's speech to the liars in the Fire, or the angels' speech by His command. They are told to taste their own punishment, the very punishment whose arrival they had mockingly demanded by asking when the Day of Retribution would come.
verses.15: Al-Mizan contrasts the Godwary with the liars: the indefinite gardens and springs hint at a magnificence beyond description, with the springs belonging within the gardens. Receiving their Lord's gifts means accepting them and being pleased with both Him and His giving. This state is explained by their earlier virtue in this world, namely their good deeds.

verses.17: Al-Mizan treats these verses as an exposition of the Godwary's virtue. Despite several grammatical analyses of mā yahjaʿūn and qalīlan, each permits the sense that they slept little: either for little of every night and spent most of it praying, or missed ṣalāt al-layl on only a few nights of their lives. Their dawn istighfār is asking forgiveness for sins, not, as a suggested reading has it, prayer. Their conduct toward others complements their conduct toward God: they considered the beggar and deprived to have a ḥaqq in their wealth out of mercy and goodness. The sāʾil openly asks from poverty, whereas the maḥrūm cannot obtain provision but refrains from asking through embarrassment.

verses.20: Al-Mizan says the signs in the earth are arguments for God's exclusive lordship, not merely for His existence or for the return of all things to Him, as the conclusion 'So flee toward God' (51:50–51) shows. Land, sea, mountains, springs, rivers, minerals, and their benefits form a harmonized, enduring system that serves animals and plants and cannot be chance or accident. This ordered whole displays the power, knowledge, and wisdom of one partnerless Creator and governor, a plain proof for people of conviction.
verses.21: Al-Mizan joins the signs in human selves to those in the earth. Bodies, limbs, cells, their coordinated action despite their many parts, and life's successive stages point to a single governing agent. The soul receives the distinct information of sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, and similarly brings diverse faculties such as anger and desire under one control, although each has its own system. Since this ordering system arose with these phenomena and did not create itself, it too is the work of a Maker. There are also indescribable spiritual signs that open certainty to the seeker and show the dominions of heaven and earth, as in (6:75).
verses.22: Al-Mizan gives several senses to provision being in the heavens: rain, which causes earthly sustenance; celestial causes such as the Sun, Moon, planets, seasons, and the succession of night and day; its inscription on the Guarded Tablet; or its descent from the Unseen, as all things descend from God in known measure (15:21). Rizq includes whatever sustains a person, from food, drink, clothing, and shelter to spouse, child, knowledge, and strength. 'What you are promised' is joined to provision and appears to mean Paradise; readings that include Hell or reward and punishment do not fit (7:40), although punishment can descend from heaven. Making the phrase a separate sentence whose predicate is (51:23) produces an overly convoluted sense.
verses.23: Al-Mizan takes 'it is indeed the truth' to refer chiefly to the preceding statement that provision and the promised Paradise are in the heavens; this is fixed in the Divine Decree as certainly as human speech. It rejects readings that restrict the pronoun to only one of them or extend it to God, the Prophet, the Qur'an, Retribution, the Day, or all that precedes. Rizq is whatever sustains a recipient or becomes attached to and adds to its existence, including food and a spouse, and belongs to the interconnected stages of physical existence governed by a complete chain of sufficient causes and necessary effects. Provision and marzūq are inseparable: neither can meaningfully exist without the other, nor can provision exceed the recipient's need. Thus provision lies within qaḍāʾ ilāhī primarily rather than accidentally, which is what makes it ḥaqq.
verses.24: Al-Mizan identifies Abraham's honoured guests as the angels who brought good news to him and his wife before destroying Lot's people, a story that contains a sign of God's sole lordship. The question magnifies the story's importance. Mukramīn describes the guests, while ḍayf remains singular because it is originally a maṣdar and does not take dual or plural forms.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains the angels' salāman as an accusative greeting implied by 'we give you peace,' while Abraham's salāmun is a nominative nominal sentence, 'peace be upon you.' His reply is therefore superior: the nominal form signifies peace already established, whereas the verbal form suggests a continuing state not yet established. The commentary takes 'an unfamiliar folk' as Abraham's inward recognition that he did not know them, not speech addressed to them; (11:70) concerns the later, visible appearance of that unease when they did not eat.
verses.26: Al-Mizan defines iḥtiyāl as retiring or going secretly. The fat calf is understood as roasted from the ensuing act of placing it before the guests, though the fa may instead mark a lapse during which Abraham slaughtered and roasted it. The angels did not eat, but Abraham took them for human beings and asked them to do so.

verses.28: Al-Mizan explains that, after the guests did not touch the food, Abraham inwardly felt khīfah, a kind of fear. Their unconnected reassurance is presented as the answer to the audience's implied question about what followed, and it changes his fear into relief and happiness through the announcement of a wise son. The commentary notes the unresolved identification of that son as Ishmael or Isaac.
verses.29: Al-Mizan cites Majmaʿ al-Bayān that ṣarrah means a shriek, originally the creaking of a door, and ṣakkah a deliberate, forceful blow. Abraham's wife therefore came out shrieking, struck her face, and protested the announcement because she was an old barren woman. The reported alternative that ṣarrah means a group is acknowledged, but the first reading better accords with the context and tone.
verses.30: Al-Mizan takes kadhālik as referring to the promised birth to Abraham and his wife despite their old age, her barrenness, and his being elderly. The angels' answer grounds that promise in the Lord's wisdom and all-encompassing knowledge, from which nothing in the matter is hidden.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains khaṭb as a momentous errand, ḥijārah min al-ṭīn as petrified clay, and taswīm as marking with a sign. Abraham asks the messenger angels their mission, and they answer that they have been sent against Lot's guilty people with marked stones, called sijīl, to destroy the profligate. The definite al-musrifīn appears to designate that particular already-mentioned group.

verses.35: Al-Mizan reads the fa as passing over the omitted stages in the angels' story: their arrival at Lot, the townspeople's demand for the guests, and the rescue of Lot and his family before the town's destruction. God found only one household of muslims, Lot's house, among its faithful. By overturning the land and destroying its people, He left an enduring sign of His lordship and the falsity of polytheism for those who fear a painful punishment.

verses.38: Al-Mizan connects the sign in Moses to the preceding signs left in destroyed peoples. His ṣulṭān mubīn is the awe-inspiring proofs and miracles with which he was sent to Pharaoh.
verses.39: Al-Mizan takes Pharaoh's rukn primarily as his armies, so that he turned away accompanied by his support; it also records the possible transitive sense that he turned his support away. His alternating accusations that Moses was mad and a sorcerer correspond to the charges recorded in (26:27) and (26:34).
verses.40: Al-Mizan explains nabdh as throwing something away without regard and mulīm as one who has acted blameworthily. God seized Pharaoh and his armies and cast them into the sea for his disbelief, obstinacy, and recalcitrance. Though his hosts shared the fate, Pharaoh alone is called mulīm because, as their leader, he led them to perdition, as (11:98) says. The account also alludes to the formidable power and violence at God's disposal.
verses.41: Al-Mizan treats the barren wind sent against ʿĀd as one deprived of the winds' usual benefits, such as bringing clouds, pollinating trees, spreading food, benefiting animals, and cleansing the air. Its sole effect was destruction.
verses.42: Al-Mizan says the barren wind left nothing it struck without reducing it to decayed bones.
verses.43: Al-Mizan again connects the account to a divine sign. Ṣāliḥ told Thamūd to enjoy themselves only briefly after they hamstrung the she-camel, giving them three days to repent of faithlessness and insolence, as in (11:65). They gained nothing from the reprieve, and punishment became due.
verses.44: Al-Mizan defines ʿatw as shrinking from obedience and thus as a form of insolence. Thamūd's defiance includes their refusal to repent during the three-day reprieve, which answers the objection that their disobedience preceded their commanded enjoyment. The thunderbolt that seized them as they watched does not conflict with the Cry in (11:67), since both a thunderbolt and a cry could have punished them together.
verses.45: Al-Mizan explains that Thamūd could not even rise from where they sat to flee when punishment overtook them, nor could anyone else help repel it. They were therefore unable to avert it either by themselves or through outside aid.
verses.46: Al-Mizan connects Noah's people to the preceding destroyed nations and takes the accusative construction to imply that God destroyed them before ʿĀd and Thamūd. Their transgression was against the divine commands and prohibitions brought through the messengers: God is the Lord of all, their religion is true, and it includes the promise of Resurrection and recompense.
verses.47: Al-Mizan returns here to the signs that began at (51:20). Ayd can mean power, so that God built the sky with immeasurable might and remains unconstrained, or blessing, so that He abounds in wealth and blessings and His stores never diminish as He distributes provision. Mūsiʿūn may also mean that He makes the heavens expand, a possibility the commentary notes alongside modern calculations.
verses.48: Al-Mizan says farash and mahd both mean to spread out. God levelled the earth so that people might dwell and live on it, yet this spreading and levelling does not contradict the earth's roundness.
verses.49: Al-Mizan understands the pairs as complementary opposites that complete one another, such as active and passive and male and female. It records broader readings that include heaven and earth, day and night, land and sea, humans and jinn, and a narrower one limited to male and female. The admonition is that the Creator of all such pairs has neither partner nor opposite and is absolutely one.
verses.50: Al-Mizan presents these verses as the conclusion to the proofs of God's sole lordship and divinity and to the accounts of destroyed deniers. To flee toward God is to seek refuge from kufr and its punishment by believing in Him alone and making Him the exclusive object of worship. The prohibition on another god explains that flight, and the repeated warning emphasizes words spoken by the Prophet himself.
verses.51: Al-Mizan presents these verses as the conclusion to the proofs of God's sole lordship and divinity and to the accounts of destroyed deniers. To flee toward God is to seek refuge from kufr and its punishment by believing in Him alone and making Him the exclusive object of worship. The prohibition on another god explains that flight, and the repeated warning emphasizes words spoken by the Prophet himself.
verses.52: Al-Mizan says kadhālik sums up the preceding denials and conflicting claims about messengers. The verse likens the Meccan polytheists to earlier peoples: whenever a messenger came, they too called him a magician or a madman.
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains tawāṣaw as a group's enjoining one another about a matter, here the recurring slanders against messengers. The question is rhetorical amazement: it asks whether earlier peoples instructed later ones to say this, then answers that their shared rebelliousness, not such coordination, produced it.
verses.54: Al-Mizan draws the command to turn away from the polytheists from their rebellion, arrogance, and stubborn rejection. Since preaching only elicits charges of magic and madness and intensifies their obstinacy, the Prophet need not dispute with them further; he has already presented every proof and is not blameworthy for leaving them.
verses.55: Al-Mizan reconciles the command to turn away with the command to admonish: the Prophet should continue reminding as before because it benefits the faithful. Unlike such admonition, disputing the rebellious polytheists benefits them not at all and only increases their disbelief.
verses.56: Al-Mizan treats the shift to divine monologue as marking a purpose of creation that belongs to God alone, unlike actions performed through intermediaries. The negation and exception establish worship as creation's purpose: jinn and humans are to be worshippers, not created to meet any need in God, who lacks no perfection. The perfection and its effects, including mercy and forgiveness, return to the act and creatures; if worship yields maʿrifah and dedication, those are its higher end. Against the objection from (11:118–119) and (7:179), the commentary says the former concerns mercy, while Hell is a secondary, not primary, purpose; a publisher's note directs readers to the earlier discussion of (7:179). It rejects taking worship as merely cosmic worship, since that belongs to all creatures and cannot explain this rebuke of faithless jinn and humans, and rejects taking it as mere capacity, since capacity is sought for actual worship. The article names the species rather than every individual, so the purpose stands while some disobey, though it would fail if none worshipped. Actual ritual worship is itself a means to the servant's humble, needy turning toward God's Presence; this is the maʿrifah meant by worship and the highest end, turning away even from oneself to remember the Lord. Accordingly, God shows no special concern for those who do not worship Him (25:77).
verses.57: Al-Mizan defines iṭʿām as providing food and reads its mention after rizq as particularizing a common and base creaturely need. One reported sense is that God neither needs people to provide for His servants, whom He Himself provides for, nor to feed Him. Another distinguishes acquiring provision from presenting it to a master: God desires neither what they acquire nor their offering of food to Him.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains the move from 'I' to 'He' as linking God's lack of need for provision to the majestic name Allāh, the source and return of all things. Razzāq is an intensive form: God is the sole provider of countless beings. Dhū al-quwwah and matīn are stronger divine names akin to al-qawiyy; together the three names establish that God alone governs provision and nothing can prevent it reaching its recipients, however numerous.
verses.59: Al-Mizan defines dhanūb as a share and takes the opening fa as a consequence of creation for worship. Wrongdoers who refuse worship receive no divine concern or felicity but a portion of punishment like that of their destroyed counterparts. They must not press God to hasten it by mockingly asking when the promised Day will come. The return from third-person to first-person speech signals that this warning concludes the preceding divine words beginning with the declaration that jinn and humans were created to worship God.
verses.60: Al-Mizan says the concluding fa follows the warning that wrongdoers have an allotted punishment. The faithless will receive that share on their promised Day of Resurrection, even if some reaches them earlier, a day containing only woe and destruction for them. Replacing 'those who do wrong' with 'the faithless' identifies their wrongdoing as kufr.
